identity.title: Optimal Sparsity of Mixture-of-Experts Language Models for Reasoning Tasks

problem.claim: How MoE sparsity, including total parameters, active parameters, and routing, affects memorization and reasoning under fixed compute budgets.

gap.claim: Dense-model scaling frontiers overlook MoE sparsity, and scaling-law coefficients can shift with architecture or data-pipeline changes.

contributions.claim: Trains MoE families varying total parameters, active parameters, and top-k routing under fixed compute to separate pre-training loss from downstream accuracy.
Identifies active FLOPs and total tokens per parameter as joint determinants of optimal MoE sparsity, with different implications for memorization and reasoning.
Releases code, data sources, and logs for reproducibility and future work.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present active FLOPs and TPP as principles that revise the classical compute-optimal scaling picture for MoE sparsity.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that, among models with identical training loss, greater active compute corresponds to higher reasoning accuracy.
The authors report that memorization improves with more parameters, whereas reasoning benefits from an optimal TPP, indicating greater data demand for reasoning.
The authors report that neither GRPO post-training nor increased test-time compute changes these trends.

narrative_sequence.summary: Architecture and data-pipeline changes can shift scaling-law coefficients, while dense frontiers omit MoE sparsity.
The study examines sparsity effects across memorization and reasoning regimes.
MoE families vary total and active parameters plus top-k routing under fixed compute budgets.
Reasoning tracks active FLOPs and optimal TPP differently from memorization; post-training and test-time compute do not alter the reported trends.
The authors argue that MoE sparsity should be optimized jointly using active FLOPs and TPP.

source_observation.claim: The abstract separates capability regimes and reports distinct scaling relationships for memorization versus reasoning, while explicitly controlling compute and disentangling loss from downstream accuracy.

lessons.interpretation: A claim becomes more informative when the capability regime, control variables, and proxy-to-outcome distinction are made explicit.
lessons.application: Frame a scaling study around regime-specific outcomes, state the main controls, and distinguish training-objective changes from downstream capability changes.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the task has no meaningful regime distinction or when the design cannot support the proposed controls.

unknowns: The abstract gives no quantitative effect sizes, model scales, task identities, or details of the fixed-compute protocols.
It does not specify how the reported optimal TPP is selected or whether the trends hold across all tested regimes and scales.
The reproducibility release is reported but not independently verified here.
